title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 22, 2026 (Three Never-Checked Scores Get Their First Real Measurement)
headline: Amsterdam, Seoul and Columbia University's scores were never checked — first measurements correct them.
summary:
Twelve organizations were checked overnight. Three of them had never been individually measured before, and first measurements now propose corrections to their published scores. Four readings held steady. Five large companies measured far below their published scores, but that finding was treated as one shared data problem, not five separate declines.

Amsterdam's published score placed it 8th of 250 cities the benchmark tracks. A first measurement reads 72 out of 100, two tiers lower — but the same review raised the city's score for something it did right. On September 19, the mayors of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague jointly asked the Dutch government for about 100 million euros a year to fight rising homelessness. Naming a problem you cannot fix alone counts as compassion working, not failing, and that letter is not why the score moved down. The lower reading instead comes from Amsterdam's own independent watchdog, which found 2,942 complaints in 2025 from residents stuck in slow procedures, and from a 4.2-million-euro fairness algorithm the city let outside researchers investigate — and then pulled itself, before any court forced it to, when the investigation found it still discriminated against residents with immigrant backgrounds.

Columbia University's published score falls to a measured 31 out of 100. Two active lawsuits accusing the university of failing to protect students were excluded from the check entirely, because they are unproven claims, not settled facts. What was used instead: a May 2025 finding by two federal agencies that Columbia showed "deliberate indifference" toward harassment of Jewish students for 19 months, and a 221-million-dollar settlement the university publishes on its own website. Columbia's score would land in the same range even if both pending lawsuits were dismissed tomorrow.

Seoul's published score falls to a measured 49 out of 100. A city official used a contractor's credit card for personal purchases for about a year before getting caught — but South Korea's national auditor caught him, not the city itself, so Seoul's own record for catching its own problems does not get credit for a fix it has not yet made.

Separately, five large U.S. companies — Waste Management, Zoetis, SEI Investments, The Hartford and Travelers — measured 13 to 34 points below their published scores. All five share a starting score that is identical, digit for digit, to dozens of unrelated companies in unrelated industries — the fingerprint of a number nobody ever actually checked. No score changes were proposed for any of the five. The finding points at a gap in the benchmark's own records, not at anything these five companies did.

Release watch: 0 sources registered — detection did not run.

topSignals.title: Amsterdam's Top-Tier Score Was Never Checked — And the Same Review Credited the City for Speaking Up
topSignals.whyItMatters: A never-checked score put Amsterdam among the world's best-performing cities. A first real measurement moved it down two tiers, while the same review credited the city for asking for help.
topSignals.description:
Amsterdam's published score of 94.4 out of 100 placed it 8th of 250 cities the benchmark tracks, in its highest tier. Nobody had individually checked that number before this review — it came from an unverified starting value.

A first measurement reads 72 out of 100, still a strong result but two tiers lower. That move is not a penalty for the city speaking up. On September 19, the mayors of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague jointly asked the Dutch national government for about 100 million euros a year to fight a "dramatic" rise in homelessness. That letter raised Amsterdam's score for detecting and naming the problem honestly.

The lower reading comes from separate evidence entirely. Amsterdam's own independent watchdog, the Ombudsman Metropool Amsterdam, logged 2,942 complaints in its 2025 annual report and found vulnerable residents get stuck in slow procedures and long waits for help with care, debt and housing — the opposite of the consistently strong performance the top tier requires. Separately, a 4.2-million-euro algorithm the city built to fairly detect welfare fraud was found, after Amsterdam gave outside researchers full access to investigate it, to still discriminate against residents with immigrant backgrounds and lower incomes. The city pulled the system itself in May 2025, before any court or regulator forced it to.

If the Dutch government funds any part of the 100-million-euro request, Amsterdam's score would be checked again and could move up.

evidence.claim: The Ombudsman Metropool Amsterdam and children's ombudsman received 2,942 complaints, notifications and signals in 2025, and found vulnerable residents get stuck in complicated rules, neighbourhood-team problems and slow procedures.

Amsterdam launched a 4.2-million-euro welfare-fraud algorithm ("Smart Check") intended to be among the fairest in the world; in May 2025 the city council suspended it after evidence showed it still discriminated against residents with migrant backgrounds and lower incomes.
On 3 June 2025 a Dutch court ruled that 28 people must be permitted to remain in Amsterdam's emergency shelter, and that the national government must continue to cover the cost.
On 19 September 2026 the mayors of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague jointly asked the Dutch national government for roughly 100 million euros in extra annual funding against homelessness.

topSignals.title: Columbia University's Measurement Rests on a Federal Finding and a Settlement, Not on Two Pending Lawsuits
topSignals.whyItMatters: Two active lawsuits against Columbia were left out of the check entirely, because they are unproven claims. The measurement instead rests on a completed federal finding and a settlement Columbia itself publishes.
topSignals.description:
Columbia University's published score of 44.5 out of 100 had never been individually checked. A first measurement reads 31 out of 100, a lower tier.

A federal lawsuit filed September 14 by Mahmoud Khalil and a student group, and a second lawsuit filed in August by other students and faculty, both claim Columbia failed to protect them from harassment. Neither claim was used in this measurement — both are pending in court, and Columbia has not been found liable in either.

What was used is already decided. On May 23, 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Education jointly found that Columbia showed "deliberate indifference" toward harassment of Jewish students for more than 19 months starting in October 2023, including that the university had no effective way to report antisemitism until the summer of 2024. Columbia then agreed to pay 221 million dollars combined to the U.S. Treasury and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — the largest public settlement the commission has reached in almost 20 years, now being paid out — and accepted outside-set rules on student discipline in exchange for restoring federal funding. Columbia publishes the settlement on its own website.

Columbia's score would land in the same tier even if both pending lawsuits were thrown out tomorrow — the measurement does not depend on them. Three of the government web pages behind the federal finding blocked automated access, so that finding is recorded as a claim tied to the government's own web address rather than as a word-for-word quote.

evidence.claim: On 23 May 2025 the HHS Office for Civil Rights and the U.S. Department of Education jointly found Columbia University violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act by acting with deliberate indifference toward harassment of Jewish students from 7 October 2023, over more than 19 months.
evidence.source: HHS Office for Civil Rights, joint Notice of Violation to Columbia University

evidence.claim: On 23 July 2025 Columbia's board of trustees formalized a settlement paying the federal government 221 million dollars combined and accepting terms including adopting the IHRA definition of antisemitism and reviewing Middle East studies programmes; Columbia publishes the agreement on its own website.

Columbia University agreed to pay 21 million dollars to resolve EEOC antisemitism charges, described by the EEOC as the largest public settlement the commission has reached in almost 20 years; the payout to affected individuals has begun.

A federal lawsuit filed 14 September 2026 by Mahmoud Khalil and the SIPA Palestine Working Group claims Columbia's deliberate indifference to harassment; this is an unproven claim and was not used in the measurement.

topSignals.title: Seoul's Card-Misuse Case Was Caught by a National Auditor, Not the City — and That Changes Who Gets the Credit
topSignals.whyItMatters: A Seoul official misused a contractor's card for a year before getting caught. Because South Korea's national auditor made the catch, not Seoul itself, the city's own record does not get credit for a fix it has not yet made.
topSignals.description:
Seoul's published score of 60.9 out of 100 had never been individually checked. A first measurement reads 49 out of 100, a lower tier.

A Seoul city official used a contractor's corporate card 51 times over about a year to buy roughly 21 million won (about 15,000 dollars) of personal goods, including a laptop for his child, after signing a 1.04-billion-won contract with that same contractor. That is Seoul's own failure: its own employee, its own contract decision, its own internal check that missed the misuse for a year.

The catch is not Seoul's. South Korea's national Board of Audit and Inspection, a body separate from the city, found the misuse, filed a criminal complaint, and recommended penalties. Seoul's own documented role so far is that it was told after the fact; the official had already retired in June. The measurement credits Seoul for being subject to a national audit system that works, but does not credit the city's own record for a correction the city has not yet been shown to have made itself.

Seoul's real strength is its welfare spending: 451.3 billion won committed over five years against loneliness and isolation deaths, and disability welfare spending raised 8.1% to 1.77 trillion won in 2025 — real, well-documented programs that keep the score from falling further.

evidence.claim: South Korea's Board of Audit and Inspection released findings on 21 September 2026 that a Seoul city division director used a contractor's corporate card 51 times to buy 21.03 million won of personal items after signing a 1.04 billion won procurement contract with the same company, and filed a criminal complaint for bribery.
evidence.source: Seoul Economic Daily (reporting the Board of Audit and Inspection)

evidence.claim: The Board of Audit and Inspection of Korea is the Republic of Korea's national constitutional audit body — the institution that caught and referred this case is national, not municipal.
evidence.source: Board of Audit and Inspection of Korea

evidence.claim: Seoul committed 451.3 billion won over five years to the "Seoul Without Loneliness" programme and created the country's first Director General of Care and Loneliness.

topSignals.title: Five Large Companies Measure Far Below Their Published Scores — Treated as One Shared Problem, Not Five
topSignals.whyItMatters: Five unrelated companies with nothing in common but a never-checked starting score all measured well below that score. The pattern points at the benchmark's own unchecked data, not at five companies getting worse.
topSignals.description:
Waste Management, Zoetis, SEI Investments, The Hartford and Travelers were checked this cycle as part of routine coverage. All five measured well below their published scores — Zoetis measured lowest, 34.1 points below its published value; Travelers measured highest of the five, still 12.8 points below its published value.

The reason is not five separate declines. All five companies' published scores were never individually checked; they came from one of two starting values assigned identically, digit for digit, to unrelated companies across unrelated industries. Waste Management and Zoetis share one starting score with nine other companies (11 total). SEI Investments, The Hartford and Travelers share a second starting score with sixteen other companies (19 total). A score that is identical across 11 or 19 unrelated companies cannot reflect real measurement of any single one of them.

Because the pattern points at the benchmark's own unchecked starting data rather than at any one company's conduct, no score change was proposed for any of the five this cycle. Instead, the finding is being treated as one shared question about whether and how the remaining 25 companies sharing these two starting scores should be checked. SEI Investments' reading carries the least confidence of the five: about a third of its measured behaviors rest on the absence of any public disclosure — its most recent sustainability report is from 2023 — rather than on documented conduct either way.

evidence.claim: SEI Investments' most recent located corporate sustainability report is for calendar year 2023; no 2024, 2025 or 2026 report was located.

sectorAlerts.sector: Global Cities — Two Top-Tier Scores Get Their First Real Check
sectorAlerts.headline: Amsterdam and Seoul both fell two tiers on first individual measurement, for very different reasons.
observations: Amsterdam (94.4 published, 72 measured): the city's score rose for its own homelessness advocacy letter, and fell on an independent watchdog finding and a discriminatory algorithm the city itself let outside researchers expose.
Seoul (60.9 published, 49 measured): a year of contractor-card misuse by a city official was caught by South Korea's national auditor, not the city, so Seoul's own record does not get the credit.
Both retain real strengths — Amsterdam's openness about its own failures, Seoul's welfare spending — that keep both scores well above the benchmark's lower tiers.

sectorAlerts.sector: Universities — A First Measurement That Excludes Two Pending Lawsuits Entirely
sectorAlerts.headline: Columbia University's first measured score rests on a completed federal finding and a public settlement, not on active lawsuits.
observations: Columbia University (44.5 published, 31 measured): a May 2025 federal deliberate-indifference finding and a 221-million-dollar settlement Columbia itself publishes drive the score; two pending lawsuits are left out as unproven claims.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — Two Readings Held Steady, Both Turning on Who Acted
sectorAlerts.headline: El Salvador and Thailand both held their published scores this cycle, for different reasons.
observations: El Salvador (15.0 published, held): the expiry of U.S. protected status for about 200,000 Salvadorans is a United States decision and does not count against the country.
Thailand (32.8 published, 29.4 measured): an exam-fraud scandal's seizures and irregularities are treated as facts; who is responsible has not yet been decided.

sectorAlerts.sector: US States — A Federal Raid Does Not Count Against the State
sectorAlerts.headline: Georgia's score held after a federal immigration raid at a private employer's plant the state was not warned about in advance.
observations: Georgia (26.9 published, held): the raid, detentions and related claim at a Hyundai plant are federal conduct; Georgia's own documented response is consistent with its existing score.

sectorAlerts.sector: AI Labs — An Individual's Speech Is Not the Company's Conduct
sectorAlerts.headline: Anthropic's score held despite a researcher's public resignation warning, because personal speech is not treated as company conduct.
observations: Anthropic (59.1 published, 57.5 measured): a researcher's resignation and public warning is that person's own speech, not the company's; no credit was given for the absence of retaliation against him.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 — One Shared Question, Not Five Downgrades
sectorAlerts.headline: Five companies sharing two never-checked starting scores all measured well below their published values; the finding was treated as one shared data question.
observations: Waste Management (77.9 published, 46.3 measured) and Zoetis (77.9 published, 43.8 measured) share one identical starting score with nine other unrelated companies.

SEI Investments (60.9 published, 31.3 measured, the least confident of the five), The Hartford (60.9 published, 43.8 measured) and Travelers (60.9 published, 48.1 measured) share a second identical starting score with sixteen other unrelated companies.
No score change was proposed for any of the five; the pattern points at the benchmark's own unchecked starting data across 30 companies, not at any one company's conduct.

methodologyNotes.name: A Never-Checked Score Moving Down Is Not a Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Three organizations checked this cycle — Amsterdam, Seoul and Columbia University — had never been individually measured before. Their published scores came from unverified starting values, not from prior research. A first measurement correcting that number describes what the benchmark did not yet know, not what the organization did differently this week.

methodologyNotes.name: The Same Event Can Raise One Reading While Separate Evidence Lowers Another
methodologyNotes.description: Amsterdam's score rose for its own advocacy letter naming a homelessness crisis and fell on separate, independent evidence about service consistency. Reporting both effects honestly, on their own separate evidence, is standard practice rather than folding them into one unexplained number.

methodologyNotes.name: Unproven Claims Are Left Out of Measurement Until They Are Decided
methodologyNotes.description: Pending lawsuits against Columbia University were left out of its measurement entirely. Only completed government findings, published settlements and other decided facts move a score; an active, undecided legal claim does not, no matter how serious the claim.

methodologyNotes.name: A Shared, Never-Checked Starting Score Across Many Companies Is One Question, Not Many Findings
methodologyNotes.description: Five Fortune 500 companies measured well below their published scores this cycle, and all five share one of two starting scores that are identical across 11 or 19 unrelated companies. Because the pattern traces to the benchmark's own unchecked starting data rather than to any one company's documented conduct, it is treated as a single shared question rather than five individual score changes.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Amsterdam, Seoul and Columbia's never-checked starting scores were each corrected as a separate first measurement this cycle, while Waste Management, Zoetis, SEI Investments, The Hartford and Travelers share identical never-checked starting scores and were treated as one shared question instead — does that distinction hold the same way across every index?
dailyOpeningQuestion.tensionFraming: Three never-checked starting scores were corrected individually this cycle, while five sharing an identical starting-score pattern were treated as one question instead.
